Main Menu Toggle Button Sections Search Toggle Button Search Search Submit Button Submit Home News & Events Press Releases Press Release October 09, 2026 Federal Reserve Board releases results of the 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances, which provides the public and policymakers with detailed insights into the economic condition of American families For release at 10:00 a.m. EDT Share The Federal Reserve Board on Friday released the results of the 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances, which provides the public and policymakers with detailed insights into the economic condition of American families. The data provide a representative picture of what Americans own, how and how much they borrow, and how they bank. The current version of the survey has been undertaken every three years since 1989 and provides the public with an extensive time series of thorough information on the economic conditions of American families. Alongside the survey data, the Board issued its summary report entitled Changes in U.S. Family Finances from 2022 to 2025 (PDF) , which examines changes in income, net worth, assets, debt, and financial vulnerability. Key findings from the 2025 survey include: Real median family income rose 7 percent between the 2022 to 2025 surveys to $82,200, while real mean family income fell 6 percent to $145,200. Families in the lower ends of the income and net worth distributions saw modest increases in median and mean income, while families in the upper ends saw declines. Between 2022 and 2025, real median net worth rose by 2 percent to $215,900, while real mean net worth rose by 7 percent to $1.24 million. Most families across the net worth and income distributions experienced increases in median and mean wealth. The homeownership rate was 66 percent in 2025, about unchanged from 2022. For families that owned a home, the median net housing value (the value of a home minus home-secured debt, such as a mortgage) rose to $230,000 in 2025 from $218,900 in 2022. Retirement plan participation, which includes account-type plans, individual retirement accounts, or defined benefit plans, was up slightly between 2022 and 2025 at around 65 percent. For families with account-type plans, mean and median balances rose. Participation in the stock market, which includes direct stock and indirect holdings, declined slightly from 58 percent in 2022 to 56 percent in 2025. Conditional on holding stock, median stock holdings grew 36 percent from $56,900 in 2022 to $77,400 in 2025. The fraction of families with any type of debt remained about stable at 77 percent. Median and mean debt outstanding remained unchanged from 2022. The fraction of families with debt payment-to-income ratios greater than 40 percent, which are families with particularly high debt payment obligations relative to their incomes, increased from 6.5 to 8.6 percent, a level last seen in the 2013 survey. In addition to the summary report, an interactive chartbook displaying changes in these financial characteristics over time is available here . Additional data from the survey, including extensive data examining other economic conditions of American families, is made available to researchers and the public here . The survey is conducted for the Board by NORC, a social science research organization at the University of Chicago. Participants in the study are chosen at random from 119 geographic areas, including metropolitan areas and rural counties across the United States, using scientific sampling procedures that aim to produce a sample representative of American families. For media inquiries, please email [email protected] or call (202) 452-2955. Changes in U.S. Family Finances from 2022 to 2025 Evidence from the Survey of Consumer Finances (PDF) Last Update:
            October 09, 2026

public_input.title: United States Department of the Treasury Announces New Appointment
public_input.body: October 9, 2026 WASHINGTON — Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent announced today a key senior appointment at the U.S. Department of the Treasury. Dr. Judy Shelton will serve as a Counselor in the Office of the Secretary. Shelton is an economist and author specializing in international financial and currency issues. She previously served as U.S. Director of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development and as Chairman of the National Endowment for Democracy. She has testified numerous times before Congress as an expert witness on international financial relations and has consulted with national security officials on global economic developments. At Treasury, Shelton will advise the Secretary on currency policy, with a particular focus on evaluating financial conditions in China. Prior to joining Treasury, Shelton served as a Senior Fellow at the Independent Institute. She also served as a Senior Research Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford University, where she authored The Coming Soviet Crash and Money Meltdown . She holds a Ph.D. in Business Administration from the University of Utah. Shelton began her professional career as a National Fellow at the Hoover Institution, where she received a postdoctoral fellowship to study the impact of Western capital on the Soviet economy. Throughout her career, she has specialized in analyzing the internal monetary and financial conditions of nations and their impact on exchange rates. ###

public_input.title: District of Arizona Charges 345 Individuals for Immigration-Related Criminal Conduct this Week
public_input.body: Press Release District of Arizona Charges 345 Individuals for Immigration-Related Criminal Conduct this Week Friday, October 9, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Arizona PHOENIX, Ariz. – During the week of enforcement operations from Oct. 3 through Oct. 9, 2026, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Arizona brought immigration-related criminal charges against 345 individuals. Specifically, the United States filed 151 cases in which aliens illegally re-entered the United States, and the United States also charged 172 aliens for illegally entering the United States. In its ongoing effort to deter unlawful immigration, the United States filed 21 cases against 22 individuals responsible for smuggling illegal aliens into and within the District of Arizona. These cases were referred or supported by federal law enforcement partners, including U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s Enforcement and Removal Operations (ICE-ERO), ICE- Homeland Security Investigations (ICE-HSI), U.S. Border Patrol, the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), the FBI, the U.S. Marshals Service (USMS), and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF). Recent matters of interest include: United States of America v. Favela-Favela. On Oct. 5, 2026, Christina Favela-Favela was charged by criminal complaint with Transportation of an Illegal Alien. On Oct. 4, Favela drove a vehicle with her three children to the San Luis, Arizona Port of Entry seeking admission to the United States. Custom and Border Patrol (CBP) officers referred Favela’s vehicle to secondary inspection. CBP officers subsequently learned that on July 7, 2026, Favela had attempted to cross into the United States via the Lukeville, Arizona Port of Entry with two children and a male alien concealed under personal items. With this knowledge, BPAs used a canine unit on Oct. 4 and found a male passenger hiding in the fetal position under personal items in the cargo area of Favela’s vehicle. CPB officers determined the male was an illegal alien without legal authority to be in the United States. [Case Number: 26-MJ-1787] United States v. Luis Angel Diaz-Jimenez. On Oct. 5, 2026, Luis Angel Diaz-Jimenez was charged by criminal complaint with Transportation of an Illegal Alien for Profit. On Oct. 2, Border Patrol Agents (BPAs) attempted to stop a Dodge Charger for an immigration inspection. Instead of yielding to BPAs, the driver, Diaz-Jimenez, accelerated, reaching speeds of approximately 100 mph before leaving the roadway, driving through a fenceline, and coming to a stop in the desert.
